doc.title: Hal Galper interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 27, 2022

title: Rising on the Boston scene and Ray Santisi's early verdict
summary: Galper explains he held the best gigs in Boston within five years of Berklee, taking Ray Santisi's job, the same man who once told him he would never play.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: All right. So how did you become the house pianist at that club in Boston?
Oh I was house pianist — eventually I was house pianist in a lot of the gigs in Boston. You mean at Lennie’s?

Well you know, as I went through the scene you know I have to digress for a minute so you pull me back. I’m doing a lot of legacy work now with digitizing a lot of bootleg records. And I have my career, my musical growth, from 1962 up through the 90s, digitized. Maybe even more than that. And I thought it took me a much longer time to get my stuff together in Boston. I went to Berklee and started in ’56, ’57, went through the summer of ’57, left in ’58. By ’62 I had all the best gigs in town. I thought it took me much longer than that but basically within five years of starting at Berklee I had my teacher’s gig. J. Ray Santisi’s gig. And when I was going to that school in Copley Square I took a couple of lessons with Ray and at the second lesson he wrote out “Moonlight in Vermont” chords and melody. The next lesson, I couldn’t read, I didn’t know what this stuff meant. He said, “Forget it kid, you’ll never play.”

My mentor in Boston. He died. Well wouldn’t you know in 1962 I was playing Monday nights with the hippest band in town, Tuesdays and Thursdays with Herb’s big band, and the rest of the week with the Herb’s small group. I had this guy’s job. And I totally forgot, he said that to me. Because one night he came up to me and he said, “Hal, do you remember what I told you on your second lesson?” I said no. “I told you ‘forget it kid, you’ll never play.’” He had no attitudes about it at all, he was just a great guy. But I learned a lesson from that too, never prejudge a student, you just never know. You never know.
